title.narrative: Hivos Regional SRHR Fund: Adolescent and Youth SRHR Initiative 2023-2026
Hivos Regional SRHR Fund: Adolescent and Youth SRHR Initiative 2023-2026

description.narrative:
1. Support and empower adolescents and young people Strengthened and empowered youth and youth led organizations increasingly defend and promote their SRHR
2. Engage and influence duty bearers Duty bearers increasingly design, adopt and implement laws and practices that promote the SRHR of adolescents and young people
3. Evidence generation Strengthened and empowered youth researchers to generate evidence on SRHR in the ESA region

The Regional SRHR Fund aims to ensure that stronger, more diverse and better-coordinated youth-led civil society organizations are able to demand and promote access to inclusive and affirming SRHR information and services for adolescents and youth. Three objectives underpin the programme: 1) Support and empower adolescents and young people; 2) Engage and influence duty bearers on SRHR; and 3) Evidence generation.

title.narrative: 2021 Second amendment Project Extension Hivos Regional SRHR Fund

description.narrative:
Hivos has been able to show good progress and to partly catch up their delay during the second year of implementation. Hivos has been able to support 22 partners in 2024 and to obtain good results across the different objectives of the programme.
Objective 1: Support and empower adolescents and young people
Through its organizational development (OD) support, the Regional SRHR Fund strengthened the leadership and institutional capacity of 13 youth led and youth focused organizations in the ESA region five in Uganda, two in Malawi and five in Kenya. The support focused on improving governance and leadership, human resources, project management, monitoring and evaluation, financial and grant management, and resource mobilization systems.
Notably, organizations such as Eastern Visionary Youths (Zambia) and Partners for Healthy Individuals and Communities (Uganda) made significant progress in financial management, including developing and implementing financial policies, addressing audit recommendations, and enhancing compliance and budgeting processes, resulting in improved transparency and institutional sustainability. The organizational support has opened up increased funding opportunities for partners, for example with TAHI (through Her Voice under Global Fund) securing additional support.
The Fund played a key role in enhancing awareness and access to SRHR information and services for adolescents and young people across the ESA region. In Kenya, Stawisha Initiative Africa from Kenya reached over 1,700 adolescents and young women through youth forums, peer education, and safe spaces that promoted informed SRHR decision making as evidenced from increased uptake of SRHR services.
The Regional SRHR Fund has enhanced the representation, participation, and visibility of youth led and youth focused organizations in national and regional SRHR policy spaces across the ESA region. One key outcome was the formation of a regional SRHR advocacy network led by Partners for Healthy Individuals and Communities (PHIC) in Uganda, which now provides a unified platform for youth led organizations to influence policy reforms across the region.
The Fund and its partners addressed harmful gender and sexual norms using peer education, storytelling, and artbased advocacy, leading to gradual shifts in community attitudes toward adolescent sexuality and bodily autonomy.
The Fund also promoted intersectional inclusion by mainstreaming Gender Equality, Diversity, and Inclusion across all partner programmes. Furthermore, it created safe dialogue spaces by constructively engaging religious and cultural leaders which is an approach aligned with Sida's social norm change framework that emphasizes dialogue and inclusion as an essential driver to sustainable attitudinal transformation.
Objective 2: Engage and influence duty bearers on SRHR
Capacity building initiatives for young advocates have strengthened youth led advocacy, influencing national policy reforms on age of consent, CSE integration, and child marriage prevention, thereby reinforcing SRHR as a recognized human right. The Fund also strategically positioned young people as credible policy actors, engaging in high level platforms such as the SADC Parliamentary Forum, EALA, and the African Union, where they have effectively held duty bearers accountable.
Moreover, evidence generated through the Youth Researchers Academy has been utilized by Ministries of Health and Education to inform SRHR policies, demonstrating growing institutional recognition of youth produced knowledge. The Fund has embedded SRHR within human rights frameworks through legal and policy reform, ensuring national alignment with instruments like the Maputo Protocol and SADC SRHR Strategy. The Funds centering of young people as rightsholders has ensured that adolescents, youth with disabilities, and LGBTQI populations can claim SRHR as a right, not a privilege.
The Fund significantly enhanced engagement with key decisionmakers by identifying and building the capacity of 12 influential SRHR champions, including six parliamentarians, two Human Rights Commissioners, one judge, one traditional leader, and two religious leaders across the ESA region.
The Fund strengthened civil society advocacy capacity by strengthening regional multisectoral collaboration to advance the SADC Model Law on Ending Child Marriages.
Objective 3: Generate evidence
The Fund and its partners strengthened SRHR accountability mechanisms through social accountability monitoring, scorecards, and budget tracking initiatives led by youth led and youth focused organizations. These efforts have enhanced transparency, citizen participation, and oversight within SRHR systems. By devolving monitoring power to youth and civil society organizations, the Fund effectively enhanced a people centered accountability ultimately fostering a demand driven mechanisms that hold duty bearers to account.
Moreover, through regional parliamentary collaborations, SRHR accountability has been institutionalized within formal governance structures, ensuring sustained oversight beyond donor cycles. The Funds SRHR scorecards, jointly developed with health ministries, have empowered civil society to serve as active watchdogs, tracking commitments and promoting evidence based advocacy for SRHR accountability.
The Fund has notably enhanced equitable access to comprehensive SRHR services across East and Southern Africa through youth led and evidence based interventions. It has improved the availability and quality of youth friendly SRHR services by strengthening referral systems, enhancing collaboration with line ministries, and integrating inclusive service delivery models. Through targeted capacity development, the Fund has empowered partners to establish safe spaces, mobile outreach initiatives, and digital information platforms, effectively reducing access barriers for adolescents, marginalized and underserved young people.
The Fund strengthened and empowered adolescents and young people in the ESA region to generate and utilize SRHR evidence through the establishment of Youth Research Academies (YRAs) in Kenya, Malawi, and Uganda. Hosted by the Kenya Medical Association (KMA), the Centre for Youth Empowerment and Civic Education (CYECE), and Restless Development Uganda (RDU), the YRAs trained 71 youth researchers in research design, data collection, analysis, and evidence based advocacy. Youth researchers developed 15 research proposals addressing critical SRHR issues including teenage pregnancy, climate change and SRHR, substance abuse, digital technology, and access to SRHR services.
